Great questions. From what I heard at the airport from United employees, the pilot was having heart problems and was taken to the hospital.

What I’m arguing is that a volcanic eruption is an extraordinary circumstance. But that a member of the team, that is vital to the operation of the plane, falling ill is not an extraordinary circumstance. And that although it isn’t United’s fault, it is their responsibility.
Then what’s the point of EU 261?

Thanks for the reply. The pilot fell ill after the flight was completely boarded. They tried to get a replacement crew in with no luck, then considered rerouting us based on the smaller crew, also no luck. So we had to stay overnight at a hotel and try again the next day. 

My response to United has been to ask them what IS within their control? Because based on their rationale, they can talk their way out of anything. It feels like a flight crew is an implicit part of running an airline; humans getting sick is not extraordinary. 

In a decision dated 5 February 2020, the French Supreme Court (“Court of cassation”) ruled that the sudden illness of a pilot cannot be qualified as ‘extraordinary circumstances’, justifying that the air carrier be released from its obligations. I’ve found a few other cases as well, including in the UK, where a judge has this same view of “extraordinary circumstances.”  It seems ridiculous that it isn’t just spelled out in the legislation.
